newsitem.title: CANADA: Stelco casts cautious eye on the future.
newsitem.headline: Stelco casts cautious eye on the future.

text.p: Stelco Inc said on Thursday it expected steel demand and prices to remain stable in the near term, buoyed by Canada's improving domestic economy, but that it was keeping a cautious eye on the future.

Stelco Chief Executive James Alfano said the Hamilton, Ontario-based steelmaker, whose profits surged 88 percent in the first quarter of 1997 from a year earlier, will continue to benefit from Canada's healthy at-home growth.
"There is more activity in steel-based sectors in Canada than there has been in some time," Alfano told reporters after the company's annual meeting.

"We can see growth at projected levels of the Canadian economy at 3.5 to four percent, (and that) it is going to show up in some improvment (in Stelco's revenues).... Provided the U.S. market continues to experience modest growth, we expect 1997 steel demand to be similar to last year." he said.
Alfano took over the reins as chief executive at the Hamilton, Ontario-based steelmaker following the meeting. He was named president and chief operating officer in June 1996.
But Alfano was reluctant to push his optimism beyond the second quarter of 1997.

"I think we'll hold reasonably stable through the first half of the year.... I think if demand is as strong, pricing should hold, if demand starts to weaken we may start to see in some commodity areas some weakening of prices," he said.
Alfano resisted shareholder pressure to reinstate Stelco's common share dividend, which was suspended in the first quarter of 1991 when the company was hit by falling revenues and profit.
"You don't want to put the dividend in one day and take it out the next. It is a longer-term view that we take," he said.
Alfano said the steelmaker was constantly reviewing plans for acquisition or divestiture but was concentrating on a "program of improvement from within (its current) units."

Stelco's consolidated cash-on-hand stood at C$176 million at the end of the first quarter, up from C$148 million at the end of 1996, and its debt to equity ratio has reached its benchmark goal of 25 to 75.
Alfano dismissed suggestions that increased domestic supply and rising imports of steel will outpace demand.

"I think all in all the new capacity that's come on in the stronger market has been nicely absorbed because of the improvement in overall steel consumption," he said. "When the new capacity will be more problematic is when the economy slumps and steel demand slumps and you've got added supply."
Alfano said that scenario would put downward pressure on prices as North American suppliers pushed to sell their steel.

He told shareholders Stelco's move to increase the mix of value-added products, including higher margin plate, cold rolled and coated steel, will hedge against new competition and future supply gluts.
